one_liner: Tiny no_std Rust crate: table-based linear-f32 to sRGB-u8 and back, several times faster than per-call powf.
what_it_does: Three functions: f32_to_srgb8 (linear f32 to 8-bit sRGB), f32x4_to_srgb8 (four at once, SSE2 on x86/x86_64) and srgb8_to_f32 (8-bit sRGB to linear f32, a const fn). They replace the textbook transfer function that calls powf per component. It is a per-value API, not an image or buffer API, and it has no C ABI; a C++ user would copy the 104-entry table and the few lines of arithmetic (CC0 is one of the license options) or use stb_image_resize2.h, which ships the identical routine.
how_it_is_fast: Linear to sRGB uses Fabien Giesen's (ryg) public-domain trick: clamp the float to [2^-13, 1-eps], use its exponent and top mantissa bits as an index into a 104-entry u32 table of packed (bias, scale) pairs, and linearly interpolate with the next 8 mantissa bits in integer arithmetic, so no powf, no division and no libm. The SSE2 version does the clamp, shifts and the multiply-add (_mm_madd_epi16) four-wide, but the four table loads stay scalar because SSE2 has no gather. sRGB to linear is a plain 256-entry f32 lookup table.
when_to_use: Rust code (including no_std, embedded or WASM) that converts individual colour components or small batches between linear float and 8-bit sRGB, e.g. writing a linear-light framebuffer to RGBA8.
Replacing per-pixel powf calls in a hand-written loop: the crate's own benchmark shows about 6.7x for f32 to u8 and about 50x for u8 to f32 against a powf reference (derived from page data).
Graphics output where the D3D11 FLOAT-to-SRGB rule (error under 0.6 on the integer side, monotonic, round-trips with the inverse) is the accuracy you need.
Building colour constants at compile time: srgb8_to_f32 is a const fn.
when_not_to_use: C or C++ projects: there is no C API, and stb_image_resize2.h already contains the identical 104-entry table (fp32_to_srgb8_tab4, stbir__linear_to_srgb_uchar) plus a 256-entry inverse table, with SIMD paths in stb itself.

When output must match a correctly rounded powf result bit for bit: f32_to_srgb8 is approximate (max error 0.544 against the exact value), so some inputs round to a neighbouring u8 compared with the reference; the source comment itself flags this for scientific or medical imaging.

Bulk image conversion on aarch64 or other non-x86 targets: f32x4_to_srgb8 falls back to four scalar calls (no NEON), and even on x86 the SSE2 path is only about 1.1x faster than four scalar calls (440 vs 482 ns/iter, derived from page data).

Anything beyond 8-bit sRGB: no 16-bit, no other transfer functions (gamma 2.2, PQ, HLG), no colour-space conversion; a request for general gamma routines (issue #1, 2022) and a portable-SIMD port (issue #3, 2024) are open without response.
Projects that need an active maintainer: last commit 2021-05-09, version 1.0.0, and the Debian i386 test failure (issue #2, 2023) has no reply.

integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.46 (MSRV badge; CI matrix includes 1.46.0); benchmarks need nightly with --cfg unstable_bench
integration.platforms: any Rust target (no_std); SSE2 four-wide path on x86/x86_64 selected at compile time when target_feature sse2 is enabled, scalar elsewhere and under Miri
integration.thread_safety: Pure functions over constant tables; no shared mutable state (not documented explicitly)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same signature shape as a hand-written powf transfer function, but f32_to_srgb8 is not bitwise identical to the rounded powf reference, NaN maps to 0 and out-of-range input is clamped

gotchas: The crate's srgb8_to_f32 table equals the x86-64 powf reference for all 256 inputs, but on Debian i386 (i686, Rust 1.66) test_from_srgb8 fails because the runtime powf reference there differs in the last digit for several entries (issue #2); the shipped table is constant, so outputs do not change, but the 'exact' claim is relative to one platform's powf.

The README benchmark loops use compile-time loop counters as inputs and include an int-to-float conversion and a division in both arms, on an unstated CPU and rustc; treat the ratios as hot-L1 best cases for 51 or 256 values per iteration, not image-pipeline throughput.

The SIMD dispatch is compile-time only: an x86 build without target_feature sse2 (for example i586 targets) silently uses the scalar path; there is no runtime CPU detection and no AVX2 or gather path.

The table index relies on get_unchecked (unsafe) after clamping; the bounds argument is documented in the source and the exhaustive all-2^32-input tests (run in CI on stable in release mode) check error bound, monotonicity and SIMD-equals-scalar.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the catalogued siblings (fast_image_resize, stb-image-resize-opt, tir, colortwist, yuv2rgb, ImageSharp) exposes a standalone sRGB transfer function; pick fast-srgb8 in Rust when you only need the per-component conversion without a resize library. In C or C++, take the same routine from stb_image_resize2.h (or the stb-image-resize-opt fork) instead.
verified_claims_summary: The README shows the crate's own nightly libtest #[bench] output: 51 linear-to-sRGB conversions in 144 ns versus 971 ns for a naive powf reference written in the same file (about 6.7x), 51 four-wide conversions in 440 ns versus 3,625 ns for four naive calls (about 8.2x) and 482 ns for four scalar fast calls, and 256 sRGB-to-linear lookups in 81 ns versus 4,026 ns (about 50x), all derived from page data. No CPU, rustc version or flags are given, and the baseline is a straw-man reference, not an incumbent library; the README prose itself claims only about 5x and 20x.
status_note: Unmaintained since 2021-05-09 (v1.0.0) but tiny, dependency-free and available under CC0-1.0, MIT or Apache-2.0, so it is easy to vendor; its 18.3M crates.io downloads came largely through palette 0.7.6, which depended on it, while palette 0.7.7 replaced it with its own palette_math crate.
